subQuestions.questionText:
INVENTORY SYSTEMS — PATEL POWER

Krisha Patel owns Patel Power, which imports alternative-energy components (WiFi UPS units) from Zhang Zapa. Periodic inventory system; weighted average valuation. A UPS unit is one component, bought and sold as a single unit. Financial year ended 28 February 2023.

Stock records for the year:
                                  | Number of sets | Cost per unit | Total cost
Opening stock (1 March 2022)       |          3 000 |          R325 | R975 000
Purchases during the year          |         48 000 |               | R15 600 000
  June 2022                        |          6 000 |          R375 | R2 250 000
  September 2022                   |         12 000 |          R425 | R5 100 000
  December 2022                    |         30 000 |          R275 | R8 250 000
Units gifted in January 2023        |          1 500 |            R0 | R0
Closing stock (28 February 2023)   |          8 200 |               |

Additional information:
(a) They sold 42 150 units during the year at R595 each.
(b) 2 000 units were returned in October (European plug point); Zhang Zapa accepted the return.
(c) In January Zhang Zapa gifted 1 500 units free of charge (based on purchase history).
(d) R81 500 was paid for carriage on purchases during the year.
(e) An employee, Mad Mak, stole UPS units throughout the year; the loss (on the weighted average method) is material and an insurance claim was lodged.

Calculate the weighted average cost of one UPS unit.
subQuestions.memoText:
Weighted average cost per unit:
(975 000 + 15 600 000 + 0 + 81 500 − 850 000) ÷ (3 000 + 48 000 + 1 500 − 2 000)
= 15 806 500 ÷ 50 500
= R313,00 per unit ✓✓✓✓✓✓

Working: less October returns 2 000 × R425 (September cost) = R850 000 from the Rand total AND 2 000 units from the count; the 1 500 gifted units add 1 500 units at R0; add carriage on purchases R81 500.

Teaching point: Weighted average = total cost of goods available (opening + net purchases + carriage + free stock at R0) ÷ total units available. Free (gifted) stock adds units without adding cost, which pulls the average cost per unit down.
subQuestions.topic: Inventory Systems - Weighted average valuation

subQuestions.questionText: Use the same information as 1.1. As part of finalising the insurance claim, determine the number of units that were stolen during the year.
subQuestions.memoText:
Units stolen:
3 000 (opening) + 48 000 (purchases) + 1 500 (gifted) − 2 000 (returns) − 8 200 (closing stock) = 42 300 units that should have been sold.
42 300 − 42 150 (actually sold) = 150 units stolen ✓✓✓✓

Teaching point: The stock loss is the difference between the units that SHOULD have been available to sell (opening + purchases + free stock − returns − closing) and the units actually sold.
subQuestions.topic: Inventory Systems - Stock loss quantity

subQuestions.questionText: Use the same information as 1.1 and 1.2.1 (150 units stolen; weighted average cost R313 per unit). There is a R1 200 excess charged on every claim. Calculate the rand value of the insurance payout.
subQuestions.memoText:
Insurance payout:
313 (from 1.1) × 150 (from 1.2.1) = R46 950
Less excess: (R1 200)
Payout = 46 950 − 1 200 = R45 750 ✓✓✓

Teaching point: The insurer pays the value of the loss (units lost × cost price) minus the policy excess; the excess is the portion the business must always carry itself.
subQuestions.topic: Inventory Systems - Insurance payout

subQuestions.questionText:
Use the same information as 1.1 to 1.2.2. Complete the Trading Statement for the year ended 28 February 2023 (Sales, Cost of sales — showing opening stock, purchases, carriage on purchases and closing stock — and Gross profit is 'do not calculate').

Reminders: 42 150 units sold at R595; weighted average cost R313 per unit; closing stock 8 200 units; October returns 2 000 × R425 = R850 000; insurance payout R46 950 (before excess) reduces purchases; carriage on purchases R81 500.
subQuestions.memoText:
TRADING STATEMENT — year ended 28 February 2023:

Sales: 42 150 × 595 = R25 079 250 ✓✓
Cost of sales: (R13 192 950) ✓ (operation)
  Opening stock: R975 000 ✓
  Purchases: 15 600 000 − 850 000 (returns) − 46 950 (stock loss removed to the insurance/loss account, from 1.2.2) = R14 703 050 ✓✓✓✓
  Carriage on purchases: R81 500 ✓
  Closing stock: 8 200 × 313 (from 1.1) = (R2 566 600) ✓✓✓
Gross profit: DO NOT CALCULATE

Teaching point: In a periodic Trading Statement, cost of sales = opening stock + net purchases + carriage on purchases − closing stock. A material stock loss is stripped out of purchases (to a loss/insurance account) so cost of sales reflects only goods actually sold.
subQuestions.topic: Inventory Systems - Trading Statement

subQuestions.questionText:
FIXED ASSETS — PATEL POWER.

Extracted balances:
                                          | 28 February 2023 | 1 March 2022
Vehicles                                   |                ? |       R1 800 000
Accumulated Depreciation on Vehicles       |       R1 063 500 |               ?

Transactions for the year ended 28 February 2023:
(a) A new vehicle was purchased during the year for R360 000.
(b) An old vehicle that cost R250 000 was sold during the year for R120 000 cash; the business made a profit of R38 750 on this sale.
(c) Vehicles are depreciated at 15% p.a. on the cost-price method. Total depreciation on all vehicles (sold, remaining and new) has been correctly calculated as R287 250.

Calculate the following amounts:
A. The carrying value of the disposed-of asset (vehicle sold)
B. Accumulated depreciation on vehicles on 1 March 2022
C. Cost price of vehicles at the end of the year (28 February 2023)
subQuestions.memoText:
A. Carrying value of the vehicle sold:
= 120 000 (proceeds) − 38 750 (profit) = R81 250 ✓✓✓
  Accumulated depreciation on the vehicle sold = 250 000 − 81 250 = R168 750.

B. Accumulated depreciation on vehicles on 1 March 2022:
= 1 063 500 (closing) + 168 750 (acc. dep. on the asset sold, removed on disposal) − 287 250 (depreciation for the year) = R945 000 ✓✓✓✓

C. Cost price of vehicles on 28 February 2023:
= 1 800 000 (opening cost) + 360 000 (new vehicle) − 250 000 (vehicle sold) = R1 910 000 ✓✓✓

Teaching point: Work the disposal from the profit and proceeds back to carrying value, then reconstruct the accumulated-depreciation and cost accounts by adding the year's movements (depreciation, additions) and removing the amounts relating to the asset sold.
subQuestions.topic: Fixed Assets - Disposal and account reconstruction

subQuestions.questionText: Use the same information as 1.4.1 and your answers there (A = R81 250; B = R945 000; C = R1 910 000). Complete the Fixed Asset note for Vehicles as it would appear in the financial statements for the year ended 28 February 2023.

  Accumulated depreciation: (R945 000) (B)

Teaching point: The fixed-asset note reconciles opening carrying value to closing carrying value through additions (add), disposals at carrying value (subtract) and depreciation (subtract).
subQuestions.topic: Fixed Assets - Tangible asset note

subQuestions.questionText:
VAT — PATEL POWER. VAT is calculated at 15%.

On 1 February 2023 the SARS (VAT) account had a CREDIT balance of R34 500. Transactions for the year ended 28 February 2023:
1. Purchased goods marked at R8 800 exclusive, before a 7½% trade discount was allowed.
2. A debtor paid R54 625 after a 5% settlement discount was allowed.
3. A debtor whose account of R6 095 had been written off as a bad debt returned to pay the full amount.

For EACH transaction, calculate the VAT amount and indicate whether it increases or decreases the amount owing to SARS.
subQuestions.memoText:
Transaction 1: (8 800 − 7½%) = 8 140 × 15/100 = R1 221 ✓✓ — DECREASE (additional input VAT on the purchase) ✓

Transaction 2: 54 625 × 5/95 = 2 875 → 2 875 × 15/115 = R375 ✓✓ — DECREASE (settlement discount allowed reverses output VAT) ✓

Transaction 3: 6 095 × 15/115 = R795 ✓ — INCREASE (output VAT reinstated on the bad debt now recovered) ✓

Teaching point: Input VAT on purchases and reversed output VAT (discount allowed) decrease what is owed to SARS; output VAT reinstated on a recovered bad debt increases it. VAT on a purchase is calculated on the price after trade discount.
subQuestions.topic: VAT - Effect of transactions on amount owing to SARS

subQuestions.questionText:
COMPANY FINANCIAL STATEMENTS — MAZIBUKO SOLUTIONS LTD

Listed company; authorised share capital 4 000 000 ordinary shares. Standard mark-up of 150% on cost. Year ended 28 February 2023.

Extracted balances on 28 February 2022: Ordinary share capital (2 750 000 shares) R17 875 000; Retained income R9 125 000.

Shares for the year ended 28 February 2023:
• 31 July 2022: issued an additional 750 000 ordinary shares at R10 each.
• 2 January 2023: bought back 150 000 ordinary shares and paid the estate of a deceased shareholder R1 710 000.

Analyse the repurchase of shares by completing the following: the general-ledger account to be debited, the account to be credited, and the amount, for each part of the entry.
subQuestions.memoText:
REPURCHASE OF 150 000 SHARES:

Average issue price before the buy-back = (17 875 000 + 7 500 000) ÷ (2 750 000 + 750 000) = 25 375 000 ÷ 3 500 000 = R7,25 per share.

Entry 1 — remove the shares from share capital at the average price:
Debit: Ordinary Share Capital | Credit: Bank | Amount: 7,25 × 150 000 = R1 087 500 ✓✓✓

Entry 2 — the premium paid above the average price:
Debit: Retained Income | Credit: Bank | Amount: 1 710 000 − 1 087 500 = R622 500 ✓✓✓
  (premium per share = 1 710 000 ÷ 150 000 = R11,40 paid; R11,40 − R7,25 = R4,15 above the average, × 150 000 = R622 500)

Teaching point: On a share buy-back, share capital is reduced by the ORIGINAL average issue price of the shares bought back; any amount paid above that average is a distribution charged against retained income.
subQuestions.topic: Company Financial Statements - Share repurchase entries

Loan: Moyo Bank (12% p.a.)        | R29 700 000   | R20 100 000

subQuestions.questionText:
MANUFACTURING — WATSON WATCHES (manufactures a specialised extreme-sport watch). Factory 400 m²; administration offices 200 m²; sales office 300 m². Year ends 28 February.

Labour:
(a) The factory supervisor took home a net annual salary of R173 760 after 34% deductions for UIF, PAYE and pension. He also has an annual medical aid deduction of R48 000.
(b) The business contributes a total of 9% of the gross earnings of all employees towards pension and UIF.

General expenses (per pre-adjustment trial balance on 28 February 2023): Rent Expense R636 480; Insurance R70 200; Security costs R104 500.
• Rent is paid one month in advance, allocated by floor space; rent was increased by R4 680 on 1 October 2022.

Calculate: (a) the indirect labour (factory supervisor's cost to the business), and (b) the annual rent expense (before allocation).
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Indirect labour (factory supervisor):
Gross salary = (173 760 + 48 000) × 100/66 = 221 760 × 100/66 = R336 000 ✓✓
Cost to the business = 336 000 + 9% of gross (30 240) = R366 240 ✓✓

(b) Rent expense for the year:
Let the old monthly rent = x. 636 480 = 7x (Mar–Sep) + 6(x + 4 680) (Oct–Feb + 1 month in advance)
636 480 = 13x + 28 080 → 608 400 = 13x → x = R46 800; new monthly rent = 51 480.
Rent for the year = 636 480 − 51 480 (one month prepaid) = R585 000 ✓✓✓✓

Teaching point: Gross up the take-home pay by the deduction percentage AND the fixed medical-aid deduction to find gross salary, then add the employer's contribution. For rent, solve for the monthly figure from the annual total and remove the prepaid month.
subQuestions.topic: Manufacturing - Labour and rent calculations

subQuestions.questionText:
MANUFACTURING — WATSON WATCHES. Balances from the financial records:
                        | 2023       | 2022
Direct (raw) materials   | R2 190 000 | R1 350 000
Indirect materials       | R250 000   | R160 000

• Raw materials worth R4 455 000 were purchased on credit.
• R200 000 of raw materials were returned to the suppliers (not of the required standard).
• Carriage of goods: import duties on raw materials R80 250; delivery of raw materials to the factory R145 000; a refund for non-delivery of raw materials R1 750.

Complete the Raw Materials note to the Production Cost Statement for the year ended 28 February 2023.
subQuestions.memoText:
RAW MATERIALS NOTE:
• Opening balance: R1 350 000
• Purchases: 4 455 000 − 200 000 (returns) = R4 255 000 ✓✓
• Carriage on purchases: 145 000 − 1 750 (refund) = R143 250 ✓✓
• Import duties: R80 250 ✓
• Less closing balance: (R2 190 000)
• Raw materials used in the production process: DO NOT CALCULATE

Teaching point: Raw materials issued to production = opening + net purchases + carriage on purchases + import duties − closing raw materials. Import duties and carriage-in are part of the cost of the materials.
subQuestions.topic: Manufacturing - Raw Materials note

subQuestions.questionText:
Use the same information as 4.1 and 4.2.1, plus:
• Indirect materials of R930 000 were purchased during the year; 15% of all indirect materials are used in the administration and sales departments, the balance in the factory.
• Water and electricity costs R6 000 per month; administration used 14%, sales 6%, and the factory uses the rest (80%).
• Insurance premiums unchanged for the year; half the insurance is allocated to the factory.
• Security costs unchanged; the February 2023 invoice has not been paid; all security costs are allocated to guarding the factory.
• Rent expense R585 000 for the year (from 4.1), allocated by floor space (factory 400 m² : admin 200 m² : sales 300 m² = 400/900 to the factory).
• Production wastage: R18 360.

Complete the Factory Overheads note.
subQuestions.memoText:
FACTORY OVERHEADS NOTE (Do not calculate the total):
• Indirect materials: (160 000 + 930 000 − 250 000) × 85% = 840 000 × 85% = R714 000 ✓✓✓
• Indirect labour: R366 240 ✓ (from 4.1)
• Rent expense: (636 480 − 51 480 prepaid) × 400/900 = 585 000 × 400/900 = R260 000 ✓✓✓
• Water & electricity: (6 000 × 12 = 72 000) × 80% = R57 600 ✓✓
• Insurance: 70 200 × 50% = R35 100 ✓✓
• Security: 104 500 + 9 500 (February 2023 accrued) = R114 000 ✓✓
• Production wastage: R18 360 ✓

Teaching point: Only the factory's share of shared costs belongs in factory overheads — apportion indirect materials, water and electricity, insurance and rent by their stated fractions, and accrue the unpaid security invoice.
subQuestions.topic: Manufacturing - Factory Overheads note

subQuestions.questionText:
Use the same information as 4.2.1. Balances: Work in progress R1 042 000 (2022) → R1 275 660 (2023); Finished goods R6 320 000 (2022) → R7 280 000 (2023). Sales totalled R16 375 000 (mark-up on cost was 150%).

Calculate the cost of production of finished goods for the year ended 28 February 2023.
subQuestions.memoText:
Cost of sales = 16 375 000 × 100/250 = R6 550 000 (mark-up 150% on cost, so cost of sales is 100/250 of sales).

Finished goods account:
6 320 000 (opening) + cost of production of finished goods (x) − 7 280 000 (closing) = 6 550 000 (cost of sales)
x = 6 550 000 + 7 280 000 − 6 320 000 = R7 510 000 ✓✓✓✓✓

Teaching point: Work cost of sales back from sales using the mark-up, then use the Finished Goods account (opening + production − closing = cost of sales) to solve for the cost of production of finished goods.
subQuestions.topic: Manufacturing - Cost of production of finished goods

subQuestions.questionText:
Use the same information as 4.3. The owners are concerned about the increase in all stock levels. Work in progress rose from R1 042 000 (2022) to R1 275 660 (2023).

Calculate the percentage increase in the work-in-progress balances.
subQuestions.memoText:
Percentage increase in work-in-progress:
(1 275 660 − 1 042 000) ÷ 1 042 000 × 100 = 233 660 ÷ 1 042 000 × 100 = 22,42% ✓✓✓

Teaching point: Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100.
subQuestions.topic: Manufacturing - Percentage change in stock

subQuestions.questionText: Use the same information as 4.4.1. Briefly explain why the increase in work-in-progress could be seen as a reason for concern.
subQuestions.memoText:
✓✓: A rising work-in-progress balance suggests the factory is backing up — partly-finished watches are piling up rather than being completed and moved to finished goods. This points to a bottleneck or breakdown in the production process.

Teaching point: Growing WIP with no matching growth in output signals that goods are getting stuck on the production line — a sign of a process or capacity problem.
subQuestions.topic: Manufacturing - Interpreting a rising WIP balance
